title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
Exam-like exercises
Allow approximately 55–70 minutes. Show intermediate states and short explanations. Solutions are intentionally omitted so you can work through these first.

Exercise 1 — A sparse three-level address space
A machine uses:

30-bit virtual byte addresses;
1 KiB pages;
three page-table levels with index widths 6, 7, and 7 bits, from root to leaf;
four-byte entries at every level.

Intermediate entries contain physical base addresses of next-level tables. Leaf entries contain data-frame numbers and flags. Complete tables are allocated; ignore alignment padding and other metadata.

A. Structure and translation

Give the address decomposition, including the bit positions of all fields.
Determine entries per table and bytes per table at each level.
A virtual address has fields:

\[
i_1=5,\quad i_2=9,\quad i_3=17,\quad d=37.
\]
The root is based at physical address 0x4000.

Root entry 5 contains next-table base 0x8000.
Entry 9 of that table contains leaf-table base 0xA000.
Leaf entry 17 maps to frame 73 and permits the access.

Calculate:

the virtual byte address;
the physical address of each of the three selected entries;
the resulting physical data address.



B. Full versus sparse allocation

For a fully populated hierarchy, calculate:

the number of tables at each level;
the total entries at each level;
the total page-table memory.

Compare this with a full flat table using four-byte entries. Explain the difference.

The process actually has allocated virtual pages only at these index triples:
\[
(0,0,0),\quad(0,0,127),\quad(0,3,2),\quad(63,127,127).
\]

Determine the number of allocated tables at each level and the total table memory.
The process additionally allocates page \((0,3,3)\). Does this require another page-table allocation? What about allocating \((0,4,0)\)? Explain.





Exercise 2 — Translation misses and missing pages
A system uses two-level page tables and 4 KiB pages.
For process P:



Virtual page
Page-table state




0
Resident in frame 8, readable


1
Resident in frame 3, readable


2
Valid and readable, but nonresident



Initially:

P’s TLB contains only page \(0\rightarrow8\).
The TLB can hold all translations used in this exercise.
One free data frame, frame 6, is available.
Page-table pages are resident.
The OS loads page 2 into frame 6 when necessary.


A. Trace the mechanisms
P performs these reads in order:
\[
0x0020,\quad0x1040,\quad0x1080,\quad0x2008,\quad0x200C.
\]

For each read, give:

virtual page and offset;
whether the initial TLB lookup hits or misses;
whether a page-table walk occurs;
whether a page fault occurs;
whether a resident data page is evicted;
the physical address after successful completion.

Give the total initial TLB misses, page faults, and data-page evictions.



B. Timing and capacity
Assume a sequential TLB lookup model with:
\[
t_{\mathrm{TLB}}=8\text{ ns},\qquad
t_{\mathrm{RAM}}=70\text{ ns},\qquad
h=0.90.
\]

Calculate hit time, resident-page miss time, and expected access time. Exclude page faults.
A separate workload repeatedly reads one byte from pages:

\[
4,5,6,7,4,5,6,7,\ldots
\]
All four pages remain resident. Its initially empty TLB is fully associative, holds three translations, and uses exact LRU. Determine the hit/miss behavior and explain whether it implies page faults.


C. Address-space identity

Process Q maps its page 0 to frame 12. Explain what could go wrong if an untagged TLB retains P’s page-0 translation when switching to Q.
Does switching between two threads of P create the same problem? Explain.





Exercise 3 — Complete FIFO, LRU, and Clock traces
A process has three initially empty frames, numbered 0, 1, and 2. All referenced pages are valid. The reference string is:
\[
A,\ B,\ C,\ A,\ D,\ B,\ E,\ A,\ B,\ C,\ D,\ E.
\]

A. FIFO and exact LRU

Simulate FIFO and exact LRU separately.
After every reference, record:

all three frame contents;
hit or fault;
victim, if any;
FIFO queue or LRU order.

Count page faults and evictions for each policy.
Identify the first reference at which their victim choices differ. Explain using their metadata.



B. Clock
Use these conventions:

The hand initially points to frame 0.
Empty frames are filled at the hand, then the hand advances.
Every loaded or referenced page has \(R=1\).
Hits leave the hand unchanged.
During replacement, clear and pass over candidates with \(R=1\).
Replace the first candidate with \(R=0\), set the new page’s bit to 1, and advance the hand.


Simulate Clock for the same complete string.
After each reference, record:

frame contents and R bits;
the hand position;
hit/fault and victim.

At the first replacement, list every frame inspected, including repeated inspections. Compare Clock’s victim with exact LRU’s.
Explain why Clock can evict a page whose last access was more recent than another resident page’s last access.

You may use this table layout separately for each policy:













Step
Reference
Frame 0
Frame 1
Frame 2
Hit/fault
Victim
Policy metadata









Exercise 4 — R-bit evidence and its cost

A. What can sampling reveal?
Four resident pages A, B, C, and D initially have:
\[
R=0,\qquad\text{last observed epoch}=0.
\]
At the end of each epoch, the OS updates the approximate timestamp of every page with \(R=1\), then clears all R bits.
The references are:



Epoch
References in chronological order




1
A, B, A


2
C, B


3
A, C




Give every page’s R bit immediately before each scan and its approximate timestamp immediately after each scan.
After epoch 3’s scan, which page would an “oldest observed epoch” policy select first?
Suppose D has already been removed and another victim must immediately be selected among A, B, and C. Which page does exact LRU choose? Which page does the epoch approximation choose?
The OS then needs to distinguish A from C. Can their epoch timestamps establish their exact LRU order? State the actual order from the reference history and explain what sampling lost.
Does accessing A ten times during epoch 3 give its R bit a different value from accessing it once?



B. Scanning overhead
A different system has:

32-bit virtual addresses;
8 KiB pages;
12 processes, each with a full flat page table;
a 2 GHz CPU;
16 CPU cycles to read, record, and clear one entry’s R bit.

Assume a single CPU executes the scans sequentially. One scan occurs per epoch.

Calculate:

entries scanned per process;
total entries;
cycles per scan;
scan time in milliseconds.

The scan must consume at most 4% of CPU time. Calculate the minimum epoch duration, measured from the start of one scan to the start of the next.
What fraction of CPU time would scanning consume with 100 ms epochs?
Explain why increasing the epoch duration solves the overhead problem while reducing recency precision.
Only a small fraction of virtual pages are resident. Does that reduce the cost under the specified full-table scanning model? What would have to change in the scanning method to exploit sparse residency?

The OS must invalidate the relevant untagged translations when changing address spaces, or use correctly managed address-space tags.


6. Switching between P’s threads
Threads sharing P’s address space use the same page mappings. Switching between them does not itself require invalidating those mappings.

B. Scanning overhead

6. Entries, cycles, and time
An 8 KiB page uses \(13\) offset bits. Thus, per process:
\[
N_{\text{process}}=2^{32-13}
=\boxed{2^{19}=524\,288\text{ entries}}.
\]
Across 12 processes:
\[
N_{\text{total}}
=12\cdot524\,288
=\boxed{6\,291\,456\text{ entries}}.

At 16 cycles per entry:
\[
C=6\,291\,456\cdot16
=\boxed{100\,663\,296\text{ cycles}}.
\]
At 2 GHz:
\[
t_{\text{scan}}
=\frac{100\,663\,296}{2\cdot10^9}
=0.050331648\text{ s}.
\]
\[
\boxed{t_{\text{scan}}\approx50.33\text{ ms}}.
\]

The epoch duration includes the scan:
\[
\frac{t_{\text{scan}}}{T}\le0.04.
\]
Therefore:
\[
T\ge\frac{0.050331648}{0.04}
=\boxed{1.2582912\text{ s}}.
\]
A practical rounded choice is 1.26 seconds or longer.


8. With 100 ms epochs
\[
\alpha
=\frac{50.331648\text{ ms}}{100\text{ ms}}
=0.50331648.
\]
\[
\boxed{\text{Scanning consumes approximately }50.33\%\text{ of CPU time}.}
\]


9. Longer epochs
Increasing \(T\) reduces the overhead fraction \(t_{\text{scan}}/T\).
However, accesses over a longer interval receive the same epoch timestamp. The approximation therefore loses more information about which page was accessed most recently.


10. Sparse residency
No reduction under the specified model. It scans every entry of every full flat table, regardless of residency.
To exploit sparse residency, the scanner would need to visit only relevant entries—for example, by maintaining a collection of resident-page mappings rather than scanning the full virtual-page range.

title: 6  Advanced paging and virtual memory
text:
Supplementary Matrial
I agree with your suggestion to keep the detailed implementation relatively low priority for now. However, after checking the uploaded materials, epoch-based LRU approximation is actually more exam-relevant than you suspected.
The IBN summary explicitly describes storing the last 8, 16, or 32 observations of each page’s R bit. Moreover, the 2016 exam (Aufgabe 2.5, 4 points) asks how hardware R bits can be used to approximate the last access time. Übungsblatt 6, Aufgabe 4 asks about scanning overhead and choosing an epoch length. 
ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf
ibn-klausur-2016.pdf
Our previous assignment-sheet analysis also classified these calculations as high priority. So I wouldn’t interpret the omission as a deliberate decision that the mechanism is unimportant. A concise explanation should have been included.

1. How epochs and shifting registers work
An epoch (Epoche) is simply a fixed time interval, for example 100 ms.
For each relevant page, the OS maintains:

The hardware-maintained R bit.
A software-maintained history register, say 8 bits long.

At the end of each epoch, the OS performs three operations:

Read the current R bit.
Shift the history register one position to the right, inserting R as the leftmost bit.
Clear R for the next epoch.

In pseudocode:
for each resident page p:
    history[p] = (history[p] >> 1) | (R[p] << 7)
    R[p] = 0
Here history[p] is an 8-bit value, and >> and << are bit shifts.

Concrete example
Suppose page A is accessed during epochs 1 and 3, but not during epochs 2 and 4.



Epoch
R observed
History after update




Initially
—
00000000


1
1
10000000


2
0
01000000


3
1
10100000


4
0
01010000



The leftmost bit represents the most recent epoch; older observations move to the right.
Compare two pages:






Figure 6.1: epoch bits



The aging algorithm treats these bit histories as unsigned integers and preferentially evicts the page with the smallest value.
In this case, B is selected.
This approximates LRU because an older reference contributes a smaller value than a recent one. It is not exact LRU: the history also reflects how many epochs contained references, and accesses within an epoch cannot be ordered.



2. Where is the history stored?
Normally, the history register is maintained by the operating system in software, not by the MMU in a dedicated hardware field.
It is useful to distinguish:








Information
Typical storage
Maintained by




R bit
Page-table entry
CPU hardware; OS can clear


M bit
Page-table entry
CPU hardware; OS manages as needed


8/16/32-bit history
Kernel-managed page metadata
Operating system



The history could be stored in an auxiliary array indexed by virtual page, or in metadata associated with resident physical pages.
Some architectures offer software-available PTE bits, but a conventional hardware-defined PTE does not provide a dedicated 8-, 16-, or 32-bit aging register.
One interesting correction to the IBN summary: it suggests an inverted page table is necessary to examine the pages of all processes. That is not generally required. The OS can scan conventional page tables belonging to different processes or maintain separate metadata structures. In fact, Übungsblatt 6, Aufgabe 4 explicitly assumes direct page tables, one per process. 
ueb06-ibn-SS2025.pdf


3. How important is this for the exam?
I would distinguish the following levels of preparation.







Knowledge
Priority




Explain that the CPU sets R on access
Very high


Explain periodic sampling and clearing of R
High


Explain storing several epochs of R-bit history
High


Calculate scanning overhead and reason about epoch length
High


Simulate a few history-register updates
Medium


Know kernel data structures and exact implementation details
Low



The trade-off for epoch length is also worth remembering:

Short epochs: Better time resolution, but more frequent scanning and therefore higher overhead.
Long epochs: Lower scanning overhead, but less precise information about recent accesses.


My recommendation
Spend enough time to understand the shifting-history mechanism and be able to explain it in 3–4 sentences. You now have sufficient background for that.
Then continue with the main Day 4 material. The detailed implementation of aging counters, page metadata, and reverse mappings can wait until after the core preparation plan.
One especially useful connection: The 2016 exam’s question about approximating last-access time can be answered directly with the R-bit sampling and history mechanism above. So this is one of those small details worth retaining, even under time pressure.

title: 7  Deadlocks and CPU scheduling
text:
Deadlocks: what actually prevents progress
The main skills today are:
This follows the Day 5 plan and Sheet 8 priorities in 15-Operating-Systems-and-Networks-SoSe-25-Notes.pdf and 08-ueb08-ibn-SS2025.pdf.
Deadlocks receive somewhat greater emphasis: the 2016 exam has an 11-point deadlock problem covering definitions, semaphore code, graphs and Banker’s main idea. Its appended older minitest also tests SJF and Round Robin. 12-ibn-klausur-2016.pdf The 2026 protocol explicitly reports graph construction followed by Banker execution; it does not explicitly report scheduling, but is an incomplete reconstruction. 13-Ged-chtnisprotokoll_Klausur_-IBN_Ersttermin.pdf
A group of processes is deadlocked (verklemmter Zustand) when every process in the group waits for an event that only another blocked process in that group can cause.
For a resource deadlock, that event is normally the release of a resource.
For example:
Neither reaches its release operations.
Ordinary blocking is different: a process can wait for a resource held by another process that is still able to finish and release it.
Starvation is also different: a process is repeatedly passed over while other processes continue making progress. In a deadlock, the participating processes cannot make progress through their normal execution.
A deadlock can involve only part of a system. Other processes may continue running.

title: 7  Deadlocks and CPU scheduling
text:
\(P_1\) holds resource \(X\) and waits for \(Y\).
\(P_2\) holds \(Y\) and waits for \(X\).
Both release their resources only after acquiring both and completing their work.






The four necessary Coffman conditions
For the resource model used here, deadlock requires all four:








Condition
Meaning
Why it matters




Mutual exclusion (wechselseitiger Ausschluss)
Each relevant resource instance can be held by only one process at a time.
If everyone could use the resource simultaneously, exclusive ownership would not block access.


Hold and wait
A process retains resources while waiting for additional ones.
Its existing allocation remains unavailable to others.


No preemption (Ununterbrechbarkeit)
Allocated resources cannot simply be taken away; the owner must release them.
The system cannot resolve the dependency by forcibly reclaiming the needed resource.


Circular wait (zyklische Wartebedingung)
There is a cyclic chain of resource dependencies between processes.
The waiting dependencies can lead back to the original process.



Mutual exclusion applies to an instance, not necessarily to an entire resource type. A type with three instances can serve three processes simultaneously.
Also, CPU preemption is different from resource preemption. Suspending a process and scheduling another does not release its mutexes or allocated devices.


Necessary does not automatically mean sufficient
Two distinctions matter:

A system may permit all four conditions without currently being deadlocked. Opposite lock orders, for example, allow a bad interleaving, but one process might acquire both locks and finish before the other starts.
With multiple instances, a graph can contain a cycle while another process can release an interchangeable instance and break the dependency.

To establish a particular deadlock, show why the relevant waiting cannot be resolved.


Preventing deadlock through acquisition order
Assign exclusive locks a global order, for example:
\[
L<M<N.
\]
Every process must acquire the locks it needs in increasing order. A process needing \(L\) and \(N\) acquires \(L\) first; one needing \(M\) and \(N\) acquires \(M\) first.
For distinct single-instance locks, a circular wait would require resource ranks to keep increasing and eventually return to the starting rank:
\[
L<M<N<L,
\]
which is impossible. This eliminates circular wait.
The rule must apply to all relevant acquisition paths. Merely changing the release order does not repair inconsistent acquisition.
Your Day 2 example in which writers acquire several permits also illustrates hold and wait: partial allocations remain held while further acquisition blocks. Ordering distinct lock types is a useful prevention rule, but it does not automatically repair repeated partial acquisition from one multi-instance semaphore.

Resource-allocation graphs
A resource-allocation graph (Ressourcenbelegungsgraph, RBG) represents both ownership and outstanding requests.

Graph situation

Consider two instances of \(X\), one instance of \(Y\), and three processes:

\(P_1\) holds one \(X\) and requests \(Y\).
\(P_2\) holds \(Y\) and requests one \(X\).
\(P_3\) holds the other \(X\) and needs nothing further.

The following compact diagram labels instance counts instead of drawing dots:

section: Executing the course’s Banker algorithm by hand
text:
Executing the course’s Banker algorithm by hand
The course procedure repeatedly asks:

Can some unmarked process obtain its additional requested resources, finish, and release its allocation?

For these hand exercises, assume that once a process receives its stated additional resources, it eventually finishes without further requests and releases everything it holds.
The eligibility test is:
\[
\boxed{R_i\leq A}
\]
component by component. There must be enough of every resource type.
For example:
\[
(1,0,2)\nleq(2,3,1),
\]
because only one instance of the third type is available. Having enough resources in total does not help.
The procedure is:

Calculate the initial \(A\).
Leave all processes unmarked.
Find an unmarked process satisfying \(R_i\leq A\).
Mark it and record its index.
Update: \[
\boxed{A\leftarrow A+C_i}.
\]
Reconsider the remaining processes with the updated \(A\).
Stop when all processes are marked or no remaining process is eligible.

This is the hand procedure used in the Sheet 8 solutions. 14-Operating-Systems-and-Networs-SoSe-25-Solutions.pdf

Why add only \(C_i\)?
Conceptually, the process first receives \(R_i\), then releases both its old and newly obtained resources:
\[
A_{\text{after}}
=A_{\text{before}}-R_i+(C_i+R_i)
=A_{\text{before}}+C_i.
\]
The newly granted resources cancel. The net increase comes from its previous allocation.


Worked reduction of the graph above

\[
P_3,\ P_2,\ P_1.
\]
There is no deadlock under the stated model.
If several processes are eligible, any may be selected unless the question specifies a rule. Completing one only increases the working availability vector, so you do not need to search through permutations or backtrack.


Interpreting the result

All marked: a complete execution sequence exists.
Some remain unmarked and none is eligible: the remaining requests cannot be resolved through this reduction; a deadlocked group remains in the current-request model. Report the unmarked processes as the course asks.

Strictly, a process holding no resources can be blocked behind a deadlocked group without belonging to its circular dependency. Distinguish that case if a question specifically asks for the core cycle.


Detection versus avoidance: the meaning of \(R\) matters
The IBN summary explicitly uses the procedure in two related ways:








Use
Meaning of \(R_i\)
Meaning of failure to find a complete sequence




Deadlock detection
Current outstanding requests
Deadlock remains under the exercise model


Deadlock avoidance / safety test
Maximum remaining additional demand until completion
The state is unsafe; guaranteed completion cannot be established



Textbooks commonly reserve “Banker’s algorithm” for avoidance using declared maximum demands. The course also calls the current-request reduction Bankieralgorithmus. For the exam, follow the supplied meaning of \(R\).
An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked: maximum future demands may never all be requested.
For avoidance, the system tentatively grants a request, updates the hypothetical allocation and availability, and runs the safety test. It grants the request permanently only if a safe completion sequence remains.

title: 7  Deadlocks and CPU scheduling
text:
CPU scheduling: the execution model
The CPU scheduler selects a process from the ready processes. A process blocked on I/O or a resource is not currently eligible.
A process normally alternates between:

a CPU burst: execution on the CPU;
an I/O phase: performing or waiting for I/O.









Process type
Typical behaviour
Scheduling implication




CPU-bound (rechenintensiv)
Long CPU bursts
Frequent switching can add overhead to long computations.


I/O-bound (I/O-intensiv)
Many short CPU bursts separated by I/O
Prompt CPU access lets it issue its next I/O operation, helping responsiveness and device utilisation.



“I/O-bound” refers especially to short CPU bursts and frequent I/O, not necessarily exceptionally long individual I/O operations.
For the calculation exercises below, use one CPU, one CPU burst per process, no I/O, and zero context-switch overhead.

FCFS — First Come, First Served
Maintain a FIFO ready queue.
When the CPU becomes free, run the process that has waited in that queue longest. It runs until its CPU burst finishes.
FCFS is non-preemptive: a new arrival does not interrupt the running process.
A long burst can delay many short ones—the convoy effect.


SJF — Shortest Job First
Whenever the CPU becomes free, select the shortest next CPU burst among processes currently ready.
For Day 5, use non-preemptive SJF, as in the course exercise. Once selected, the process finishes its burst even if a shorter process arrives meanwhile.

If all processes are ready initially, sort them by burst length.
With different arrival times, reconsider only the processes that have arrived whenever the CPU becomes free.

Use a stated tie rule, such as earlier arrival, then lower process index.
When all jobs are available initially, burst lengths are known, and overhead is ignored, SJF minimises average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules. Putting a short job before a long one reduces how long that short job waits.
Real systems usually have to estimate future burst lengths.


Round Robin — RR
Maintain a FIFO ready queue and choose a positive time quantum \(q\).
For each CPU allocation:

Remove the process at the front.
Run it for: \[
\Delta t=\min(q,\text{remaining burst}).
\]
If it finishes, remove it permanently.
Otherwise, put it at the back of the ready queue.

Newly arriving processes join the back. They do not interrupt the current slice.
If an arrival coincides exactly with quantum expiry, the ordering can depend on the chosen convention. State the convention and apply it consistently.
A process that finishes early uses only the time it needs; the unused part of its quantum is not an idle interval.

Effect of the quantum

Small \(q\): frequent opportunities to run, but more context-switch overhead in a real system.
Large \(q\): fewer switches, but longer delays between turns.
If \(q\) is at least every burst length in these one-burst exercises, RR behaves like FCFS.

RR gives regular CPU access to ready processes; it does not necessarily minimise average waiting time.

title: 7  Deadlocks and CPU scheduling
text:
Gantt diagrams and time calculations
A Gantt diagram places labelled execution intervals along a time axis. Mark every boundary at which execution changes. Include an idle interval if no process is ready.
For scheduling, use:







Symbol
Meaning




\(a_i\)
Arrival time


\(b_i\)
Total CPU burst


\(f_i\)
Completion time: end of the process’s last execution interval


\(T_i\)
Turnaround time (Durchlaufzeit)


\(W_i\)
Total waiting time (Wartezeit)



The formulas are:
\[
\boxed{T_i=f_i-a_i}
\]
and, for these one-burst exercises without I/O:
\[
\boxed{W_i=T_i-b_i=f_i-a_i-b_i}.
\]
Average waiting time:
\[
\boxed{\overline W=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}W_i}.
\]
If every arrival is at zero, \(T_i=f_i\). Otherwise, completion time and turnaround time differ.
Waiting time includes all time spent ready but not running. For non-preemptive execution, it is simply start time minus arrival time. Under RR, it also includes the waits between slices.
In the short RR example, \(P_1\) starts immediately but then waits from \(t=2\) to \(t=5\):
\[
W_1=6-0-3=3\text{ ms}.
\]
Its first-start delay is zero. That delay, often called response time, is different from total waiting time.
The formula \(W=T-b\) relies on the exercise’s no-I/O model. In a general process, turnaround time also contains blocked time.

A reliable manual procedure

Write down arrivals, bursts, policy, quantum and tie rules.
Track the ready set; for RR, also track queue order and remaining bursts.
Construct the complete execution timeline.
Read each \(f_i\) from its last interval.
Calculate \(T_i\), then \(W_i\), then the average.

Check that:

no process runs before arriving;
each process receives exactly its stated burst;
no waiting time is negative;
with no idle time or overhead, final completion equals the sum of all bursts.



Fairness and starvation
Under the usual assumptions of finite bursts and a functioning scheduler:







Policy
Can a ready process starve?




FCFS
No: new arrivals cannot overtake it.


SJF
Yes: a continuing stream of short jobs can indefinitely postpone a long job.


RR
No: the FIFO queue repeatedly gives it a turn.


Fixed-priority scheduling
Yes: continuing higher-priority work can postpone it indefinitely.



In a finite closed exercise set, SJF eventually runs every process. Its starvation risk concerns continuing arrivals.
Sheet 8 A6 names three algorithms despite later saying “four”; use FCFS, SJF and RR.

title: 7  Deadlocks and CPU scheduling
text:
Common exam traps

Giving code that can deadlock without showing an actual blocking interleaving.
Claiming every graph cycle proves deadlock, without checking instance counts.
Reversing request and allocation arrows.
Treating \(E\) as free resources, or treating \(R_i\) as including resources already held.
Comparing resource-vector totals instead of comparing every component.
Updating \(A\) incorrectly: after marking a process, use \(A+C_i\), and reconsider previously ineligible processes.
Treating non-preemptive SJF as preemptive, or choosing a job that has not arrived.
Retaining a completed process in an RR queue, or giving it a full quantum after it finishes.
Confusing completion with turnaround, or first-start delay with total waiting.

The resulting dependencies are:
\[

P_3\text{ waits for }P_1.
\]
All three are blocked before work() and before their release operations.
Other interleavings are equally valid if they establish these holdings and blocked requests.


Definition and Coffman conditions
Definition: A group of processes is deadlocked when every process in the group waits for an event that only another blocked process in that group can cause.
Here, those events are resource releases.







Condition
Explanation in this execution




Mutual exclusion
Each semaphore has one permit, so each resource can be held by only one process.


Hold and wait
Each process retains its first resource while waiting for its second.


No preemption
Resources are released through signal; they cannot be forcibly reclaimed under the assumptions.


Circular wait
\(P_1\rightarrow P_2\rightarrow P_3\rightarrow P_1\).





Why more CPU turns do not help
Each process is blocked at its second wait. It cannot execute the later signal operations until that wait succeeds.
Scheduling another process does not release the resource held by the suspended process. CPU scheduling cannot break this resource dependency.


Repair through a global acquisition order
Choose:
\[
L<M<N.
\]
Every process acquires its required resources in increasing order:
P1:
    wait(L)
    wait(M)
    work()
    signal(M)
    signal(L)

P2:
    wait(M)
    wait(N)
    work()
    signal(N)
    signal(M)

P3:
    wait(L)
    wait(N)
    work()
    signal(N)
    signal(L)
Only \(P_3\)’s acquisition order needed changing.
A circular wait would now require resource ranks to increase around a cycle and return to the starting rank, which is impossible.
Releasing in reverse order is conventional. Consistent acquisition ordering is what prevents this deadlock.


Would FIFO semaphores repair it?
No.
FIFO determines which waiting process receives a permit when one becomes available. Here, no process can reach its release operations, so no permit becomes available.
Fairness does not eliminate this circular wait.

title: 8  File systems
text:
1. Foundations: names, metadata and stored data
Today’s three central skills are:
The scope follows your Day 6 plan and the Sheet 7 analysis in 15-Operating-Systems-and-Networks-SoSe-25-Notes.pdf.
The strongest direct evidence for maximum-file-size calculations is Aufgabe 6 of the 2012 mini-test appended to the 2016 exam PDF. The recent memory protocol confirms that both i-nodes and FAT appeared, but does not reconstruct their exact subquestions. 12-ibn-klausur-2016.pdf 13-Ged-chtnisprotokoll_Klausur_-IBN_Ersttermin.pdf
A regular file (reguläre Datei) is, conceptually, a persistent sequence of bytes. Its file size is the length of that sequence.
The filesystem must manage two kinds of information:
Storage is divided into fixed-size units:
For calculations, use the block or cluster size stated in the question. Hardware sector details are unnecessary here.
A file’s consecutive logical blocks can occupy nonconsecutive storage locations. For example, its first three blocks might be stored in blocks 18, 4 and 29. The filesystem’s metadata preserves their logical order.
This is the useful connection to paging: logical units need not occupy consecutive physical locations; a mapping records where each unit is stored.

title: 8  File systems
text:
Information
Examples




File contents
Text, image bytes, executable code


Metadata
File size, type, permissions, owner, timestamps, locations of stored data





A filesystem block (Dateisystemblock, often simply Plattenblock in these exercises) is a unit used to store data or filesystem metadata.
In FAT, the allocation unit is called a cluster. A cluster consists of one or more disk sectors.





Directories and filenames
A directory (Verzeichnis) stores entries associating names with filesystem objects.
In the i-node model:
\[
\boxed{\text{directory entry: name}\longrightarrow\text{i-node number}}
\]
The i-node number identifies the object’s i-node within that filesystem. The filesystem uses that number to locate the i-node.
The filename normally belongs to the directory entry, not to the file’s i-node.
A directory itself also has an i-node. Its data blocks contain its directory entries; its i-node identifies those blocks and stores the directory’s metadata.
The terminology and allocation models here follow Chapter 10 of the course summary. 01-ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf


Hard links and symbolic links









Hard link (harter Link)
Symbolic link (symbolischer Link)




What it represents
Another directory entry referring to the same i-node
A separate filesystem object storing a target pathname


File contents
Shared: both names identify the same file
Access requires resolving the stored target path


If another name is deleted
Remains valid
Can become dangling if its target pathname disappears


Filesystem boundary
Normally restricted to the same filesystem
Can refer across filesystem boundaries



Two hard links are two names for one file, not two copies. Neither name has a privileged “original” status.
A symbolic link depends on a pathname. If that pathname disappears, the link can fail even when the target file remains accessible through a different hard link.

title: 8  File systems
section: 2. FAT: a linked list represented by a table
text:
2. FAT: a linked list represented by a table
FAT means File Allocation Table.
The central structure is a table indexed by cluster number:
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{FAT}[k]\text{ describes what follows cluster }k}
\]
In a simplified model, an entry contains:



Entry value
Meaning




A cluster index \(j\)
The next cluster of this file is \(j\)


EOC
End of chain: this is the last cluster


FREE
This cluster is available for allocation



EOC and FREE are conceptual markers. Do not assume that a particular number, such as 0, always means either one. Use the question’s convention.
Sheet 7 A2’s simulator uses a separate occupancy bitfield: bit 1 means occupied, bit 0 means free. In that representation, the bitfield tells you whether a cluster is allocated, while the pointer table supplies the chain.
A FAT directory entry provides the file’s first cluster and file size. The FAT then determines the remaining clusters.

Following a chain
Suppose a file starts at cluster 4 and:
\[
\operatorname{FAT}[4]=10,\qquad
\operatorname{FAT}[10]=7,\qquad
\operatorname{FAT}[7]=\text{EOC}.
\]
Its cluster sequence is:
\[
4\longrightarrow10\longrightarrow7.
\]
Therefore:

the first logical portion of the file is in cluster 4;
the second is in cluster 10;
the third is in cluster 7.

Cluster 7 belongs to the file. EOC terminates the chain after that cluster; it is not another cluster.
A reliable hand-tracing procedure is:

Start with the first-cluster index.
Record that cluster.
Look up its FAT entry.
If the entry contains another index, continue there.
Stop at EOC; flag invalid entries or repeated clusters.

The next-cluster pointer is stored in the FAT, not inside the file’s data cluster. Consequently, if the FAT is in memory, following its pointers does not require reading each preceding data cluster.


Calculating required clusters
For file size \(S\) bytes and cluster size \(C\) bytes:
\[
\boxed{n=\left\lceil\frac{S}{C}\right\rceil}
\]
The ceiling matters because a partially filled final cluster still occupies one complete cluster.
Under the simple model without preallocation:
\[
\text{allocated data space}=nC,
\]
\[
\text{unused space in the final cluster}=nC-S.
\]
For example, with \(S=2500\) bytes and \(C=1024\) bytes:
\[
n=\left\lceil2500/1024\right\rceil=3,
\]
\[
\text{allocated space}=3072\text{ bytes},\qquad
\text{unused space}=572\text{ bytes}.
\]
That unused space is internal fragmentation. An empty file needs zero data clusters in this model.


Allocation and file growth
To allocate a new file requiring three clusters:

Find three free clusters.
Mark them occupied.
Link the first to the second and the second to the third.
Mark the third as EOC.
Store the first-cluster index and file size in the directory entry.

The clusters need not be adjacent. Sheet 7’s allocation rule chooses the free cluster with the smallest index whenever another cluster is needed. That is a rule of the exercise, not a requirement of FAT itself.
To extend an existing file:

Calculate the new total cluster requirement.
Compare it with the existing chain length.
Allocate any additional clusters.
Replace the old last cluster’s EOC with a pointer to the first new cluster.
Link the new clusters and terminate the new last cluster with EOC.
Update the file size.

Growth does not always require another cluster: the existing final cluster may still have unused space.


Invalid states worth recognizing
A small FAT problem may contain:

a cycle: traversal revisits a cluster;
a pointer to a free cluster;
an out-of-range cluster index;
a chain too short to contain the stated file size;
two independent files incorrectly sharing an allocated cluster.

A cluster ending in EOC is occupied. Also, the clusters belonging to a file are those reached through its chain—not every occupied cluster in the table.
These mechanisms are the exam-relevant core of Sheet 7 A2; its class design and simulator implementation are separate practical work. 07-ueb07-ibn-SS2025.pdf

title: 8  File systems
text:
3. I-nodes and file-block addressing
An i-node (I-Node) is a per-file metadata structure containing information such as:

file type and permissions;
owner and timestamps;
file size and hard-link count;
addresses used to locate the file’s data blocks.

The i-node is neither the filename nor the file’s contents.

Direct and indirect pointers
A direct pointer in the i-node identifies one data block.
A single-indirect pointer identifies a block containing addresses of data blocks.
A double-indirect pointer identifies a block containing addresses of single-indirect blocks. Those blocks then contain addresses of data blocks.








Pointer in the i-node
What it first points to
Data blocks reachable through it




Direct
One data block
\(1\)


Single-indirect
One block of data-block addresses
\(m\)


Double-indirect
One block of addresses of single-indirect blocks
\(m^2\)


Triple-indirect
One further pointer-block level
\(m^3\)



Here, \(m\) is the number of addresses that fit in one pointer block.
Indirect blocks contain block addresses, not additional file i-nodes. The summary’s wording about “other i-nodes” is imprecise here.
Small files can use only direct pointers. Larger files use indirect blocks as needed, allowing the i-node to describe a large file without storing every data-block address inside the i-node itself.
Unlike FAT’s global next-cluster table, this is a per-file block mapping.


Deriving maximum file size
Let:

\(B\): block size in bytes;
\(p\): size of one block address in bytes;
\(d\): number of direct pointers;
\(s\): number of single-indirect pointers;
\(t\): number of double-indirect pointers.

Assume pointer blocks contain only addresses, enough storage is available, and no other limit restricts file size.
Step 1 — Addresses per indirect block
\[
\boxed{m=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{p}\right\rfloor}
\]
Usually \(B\) is divisible by \(p\), so \(m=B/p\).
If an address size is given in bits, convert it to bytes first.
Step 2 — Count reachable data blocks separately
\[
N_{\text{direct}}=d,
\]
\[
N_{\text{single}}=sm,
\]
\[
N_{\text{double}}=tm^2.
\]
Every extra indirection level multiplies the reach of one pointer by \(m\).
Step 3 — Add the data-block capacities
For direct, single- and double-indirect pointers:
\[
N=d+sm+tm^2.
\]
A triple-indirect contribution would be its number of pointers multiplied by \(m^3\).
Step 4 — Convert blocks to file bytes
\[
\boxed{S_{\max}=NB}
\]
The method is:
\[
\boxed{
\text{addresses per pointer block}
\rightarrow
\text{reachable data blocks}
\rightarrow
\text{total data blocks}
\rightarrow
\text{file bytes}
}
\]


Short worked example
Suppose an i-node has six direct pointers and one single-indirect pointer, with:
\[
B=1\text{ KiB}=1024\text{ bytes},\qquad p=4\text{ bytes}.
\]
Then:
\[
m=1024/4=256,
\]
\[
N=6+256=262,
\]
\[
S_{\max}=262\cdot1024=268\,288\text{ bytes}=262\text{ KiB}.
\]
The single-indirect block occupies storage, but its bytes contain pointers. They do not contribute to the file’s contents.


File capacity versus total storage occupied
These are different questions:

Maximum file size: count reachable data blocks.
Total allocated storage: count data blocks plus allocated pointer blocks, and include the i-node only if requested.

For example, if a file uses eight direct data blocks and three additional data blocks through one single-indirect pointer, it occupies:
\[
11\text{ data blocks}+1\text{ pointer block},
\]
excluding the i-node itself.
Do not subtract the pointer block from the eleven data blocks. It is additional storage.


Finding the block containing a file byte
For a zero-based byte offset \(x\):
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{B}\right\rfloor,\qquad
r=x\bmod B.
\]
Here, \(q\) is the logical file-block number and \(r\) the byte offset within it.
With \(d\) direct pointers followed by single-indirect pointers:

\(0\le q<d\): use direct pointer \(q\);
otherwise, set \(u=q-d\);
single-indirect pointer number: \[
\left\lfloor u/m\right\rfloor;
\]
address position inside that pointer block: \[
u\bmod m.
\]

All indices here are zero-based.
If the i-node is cached but the required blocks are not, reading a data block takes one read through a direct pointer, two through single indirection, or three through double indirection: the required pointer blocks, followed by the data block.

title: 8  File systems
text:
4. Directories and pathname resolution
Consider:
/a/b/c/file
The leading / starts lookup at the root directory. It is not an additional named component.
For each component, the system needs to:

inspect the current directory’s contents to find the name;
obtain the child’s i-node number from its directory entry;
load the child’s i-node if it is needed and not already cached;
use that child as the current directory for the next component.

The sequence is:



Name sought
Directory searched
Child i-node obtained




a
/
/a


b
/a
/a/b


c
/a/b
/a/b/c


file
/a/b/c
/a/b/c/file



The current directory’s i-node tells you where its directory blocks are. Its directory blocks tell you which i-node number belongs to the requested name.
Having the root i-node in memory therefore does not imply that the root directory’s entries are already in memory.

A reusable disk-operation counting procedure
Before counting, establish:

Which i-nodes are cached?
Which directory blocks are cached?
How many directory blocks must be searched?
Are those blocks directly addressed?
Does the task stop at the final i-node, or also require file contents?
Do reads remain cached for subsequent lookups?

Then make one row per pathname component:









Component
Current directory
Directory reads needed
Child i-node read needed





For each row:

Count the uncached directory blocks needed to find the entry.
Obtain the child’s i-node number.
Count a read if that child i-node must be loaded and is uncached.
Update the cache state.

Finally, add any requested reads of the target file’s data or indirect blocks.
Use the exercise’s operation model. In Sheet 7 A5, an i-node read and a block read each count as one operation.


Short worked example
Find the i-node for:
/lab/report.txt
Assume:

only the root i-node is cached;
each directory occupies one directly addressed block;
every uncached i-node or block requires one read;
no additional name-lookup cache is available.




Component
Directory-block read
Child i-node read
Total




lab
Root directory: 1
lab i-node: 1
2


report.txt
lab directory: 1
report.txt i-node: 1
2



Total:
\[
4\text{ disk operations}.
\]
No contents of report.txt have been read.
If the lab i-node were already cached, the total would be 3. Its directory block would still need reading.


When “two operations per component” applies
For \(k\) components, the result is \(2k\) only when:

the root i-node is already cached;
every directory search needs one uncached block;
every child i-node is uncached and must be loaded;
no additional pointer-block reads or lookup shortcuts are needed.

If the root i-node also needs loading, add one.
If the question asks only for the final i-node number, the last directory entry already provides it; loading the final i-node is a separate action.
If the task requests the first file byte, add the necessary data-block read—and any uncached indirect blocks needed to reach it.
This directory-read/i-node-read distinction matches Sheet 7 A5 and its supplied solution. 14-Operating-Systems-and-Networs-SoSe-25-Solutions.pdf

title: 8  File systems
text:
5. Common exam traps

Reversing FAT’s meaning: FAT[k] = j means cluster \(j\) follows cluster \(k\).
Omitting the last cluster: the cluster whose entry contains EOC belongs to the file.
Rounding down: a partially filled final block or cluster still needs allocation.
Confusing names with i-nodes: several directory entries can identify the same i-node.
Counting pointer blocks as file capacity: their bytes contain addresses, not file contents.
Miscounting indirection: one single-indirect pointer reaches \(m\) data blocks; one double-indirect pointer reaches \(m^2\).
Equating cached i-node with cached directory contents: they are separate structures.
Reading beyond the requested endpoint: obtaining the target i-node does not require reading the target file’s contents.

Use units explicitly:
\[
1\text{ KiB}=1024\text{ bytes},\qquad
1\text{ MiB}=1024^2\text{ bytes},\qquad
8\text{ bits}=1\text{ byte}.
\]

\[

The new size is 10 500 bytes:
\[
n_{\text{new}}=\left\lceil\frac{10\,500}{2048}\right\rceil=6.
\]
The file already has three clusters, so it needs:
\[
\boxed{6-3=3\text{ additional clusters}}.
\]

\[
\boxed{0,\ 2,\ 5}
\]
in that order.

\]
\[

\]

Remember that cluster 0 is a valid data cluster in this exercise.

The file size is:
\[

\[

the file needs:

2.5 — Adding a double-indirect pointer (2 points)
One double-indirect pointer reaches:
\[
m^2=512^2=262\,144\text{ data blocks}.
\]
Its additional file-data capacity is:
\[
262\,144\cdot4096
=\boxed{1\,073\,741\,824\text{ bytes}=1\text{ GiB}}.
\]
The new total number of addressable data blocks is:
\[
8+2\cdot512+512^2=263\,176.
\]
Thus:
\[
\boxed{S_{\max,\text{new}}=263\,176\cdot4096
=1\,077\,968\,896\text{ bytes}}.
\]
Equivalently:
\[
\boxed{1028.03125\text{ MiB}
=1\text{ GiB}+4.03125\text{ MiB}}.
\]
The double-indirect traversal works as follows:

The i-node points to the double-indirect block.
One of its 512 addresses selects a single-indirect block.
One of that block’s 512 addresses selects a data block.

Therefore, it reaches \(512\cdot512\) data blocks. Both pointer-block levels contain metadata.

title: 9  Network stack
text:
1. Layers: different services and different endpoints
The unit below focuses on encapsulation, addressing across router hops, and IPv4 fragmentation, followed by three integrated exercises with numbered subparts.
A reusable copy is available here: day-7-network-stack.mdday-7-network-stack.md.
The scope follows the ten-day plan in 15-Operating-Systems-and-Networks-SoSe-25-Notes.pdf and A4/A9 in 09-ueb09-ibn-SS2025.pdf. The strongest direct calibration is Aufgabe 4, worth 8 points, in 12-ibn-klausur-2016.pdf; its appended mini-test also supports the TCP demultiplexing exercise. Layer terminology follows 01-ibn-zusammenfassung.pdf.
The networking questions reported in 13-Ged-chtnisprotokoll_Klausur_-IBN_Ersttermin.pdf concern subnetting, forwarding and Dijkstra, which remain for Days 8–9. The uploaded 14-Operating-Systems-and-Networs-SoSe-25-Solutions.pdf skips Sheet 9, so I have independently checked the calculations.
A network application needs several problems solved:
The protocol stack assigns these problems to different layers.
A service is what a layer offers to the layer above. A protocol specifies how participants at that layer communicate: message formats and rules for processing them. Participants communicate logically with their peers, while actual transmission uses the lower layers.
The course uses five Internet layers. Here we concentrate on the upper four; the physical layer (Bitübertragungsschicht) carries bits through the transmission medium.
A PDU (protocol data unit) is the unit handled by a particular layer, including that protocol’s control information. “Packet” is often used loosely; in an exam, identify the layer and use its specific PDU name.

Application identifiers depend on the application
Two useful examples for Sheet 9 A4:

Web: a browser communicates with a web service. A URL such as http://example.org/notes identifies a server/service and resource. DNS can resolve the hostname to an IP address; the resource path /notes is interpreted at the application layer.
Email: users/accounts are logical endpoints. An address such as igor@example.org identifies the recipient mailbox. SMTP transfers messages between mail-system processes; a transport port does not identify the recipient account.

There is no universal application-layer address field shared by all applications. Application identifiers belong to the application’s message format and semantics.


Ports, IP addresses and MAC addresses answer different questions

IP address: which destination host/interface should receive this IP datagram?
Port number: which transport endpoint on that host should receive its data?
MAC address: which interface should receive this frame on the current Ethernet network?

A port is a 16-bit transport identifier, not an operating-system PID.
A process uses a socket, the software interface through which it sends and receives network data. One process can use multiple sockets; one TCP server port can serve multiple connections.
For a basic transport endpoint, think:
\[
\boxed{\text{IP address}+\text{port}+\text{transport protocol}}
\]
Port 9000 on two different hosts does not identify the same endpoint. TCP port 9000 and UDP port 9000 also belong to different protocol namespaces.


TCP and UDP: the necessary distinction
IP provides a best-effort datagram service: delivery, order and freedom from duplication are not guaranteed.

TCP




Adds ports and preserves message boundaries
Provides a connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream


Does not itself provide reliable delivery or retransmission
Can divide stream data among multiple segments


Application sends individual UDP datagrams
Application message boundaries are not preserved automatically



Both use source and destination ports. TCP’s detailed reliability mechanisms are outside today’s core scope.

A higher-layer header becomes part of the lower layer’s payload.
Thus:

UDP payload = application message;

For the unfragmented UDP case, the frame’s conceptual order is:

Ethernet’s trailer is the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) for error detection. If an exam asks only for the layer headers, the essential order is:
link → network → transport → application message
An application message can already contain application headers, such as HTTP fields. Do not invent an additional universal application header if the question simply supplies message \(N\).

How the receiving host delivers data upward
Decapsulation removes the wrapping; demultiplexing selects the appropriate next protocol or endpoint.
For an ordinary unicast Ethernet/IPv4/UDP message:

Link layer: accepts the addressed frame, checks its link control information and extracts the IP datagram. Ethernet’s EtherType identifies the payload protocol, such as IPv4.
IP layer: processes the datagram. Its Protocol field identifies UDP or TCP: UDP is 17, TCP is 6. If fragmented, IP first reassembles the datagram before transport delivery.
Transport layer: uses addressing information to select a socket and passes the data to its application.
Application layer: interprets the message according to its application protocol.

In the basic course model, UDP delivery selects a receiving socket using the destination IP and destination port, within UDP.
An established TCP connection is distinguished by the four-tuple:
\[
\boxed{
(\text{source IP},\text{source port},
\text{destination IP},\text{destination port})
}
\]
Consequently, several established TCP connections can share the server’s local port. Their remote IP addresses and/or ports distinguish them.
A TCP listening socket accepts new connections; established connection sockets carry each connection’s data.

section: 3. Hosts, routers and the next hop
text:
3. Hosts, routers and the next hop
The ultimate IP destination and the next link-layer recipient need not be the same device.

Local destination versus remote destination
In the ordinary single-LAN setting used in these problems, the host compares the destination’s network part with its own, using its configured subnet mask/prefix.
Conceptually, with subnet mask \(S\):
\[
(IP_{\mathrm{dest}}\mathbin{\&}S)
=
(IP_{\mathrm{local}}\mathbin{\&}S)
\]
means the destination is on the same configured subnet. Here \(\&\) means bitwise AND. Detailed mask calculations belong to Day 8.








Destination
IP datagram’s destination
Ethernet frame’s destination




Another host on the same local Ethernet network
That host’s IP
That host’s MAC


A remote host reached through the gateway
The remote host’s IP
The gateway’s local interface MAC



The gateway’s IP helps identify the next hop. It does not replace the remote host’s IP in the original data datagram.


ARP: obtaining the next-hop MAC
For IPv4 over Ethernet, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps a known local next-hop IP address to its MAC address.
The sender first checks its ARP cache. If the mapping is missing, it broadcasts an ARP request on the local network. The node owning the requested IP replies with its MAC, and the sender can cache the mapping. rfc-editor.org
Therefore:

Local delivery: resolve the destination host’s IP.
Remote delivery through a gateway: resolve the gateway’s local IP.

A host does not broadcast ARP across the Internet to discover a remote host’s MAC.


What a forwarding router does
Consider A → R → B, with A and B on different Ethernet networks. Assume no address translation (NAT), tunneling or fragmentation.



Link
Source MAC
Destination MAC
Source IP
Destination IP




A → R
A’s MAC
R’s incoming-interface MAC
A’s IP
B’s IP


R → B
R’s outgoing-interface MAC
B’s MAC
A’s IP
B’s IP



The router:

Receives the frame addressed to its incoming interface and removes the link-layer wrapping.
Examines the IP destination and selects an outgoing interface/next hop.
Decrements IPv4 TTL and updates the IPv4 header checksum.
Creates a new link-layer frame suitable for the outgoing link, addressed to the next hop.

If another router follows, the new destination MAC is that router’s receiving-interface MAC. Only on the last local network is the destination MAC normally B’s MAC.
Source/destination IP addresses and transport ports normally remain associated with A and B throughout forwarding. Link-layer addresses change at router hops.
The whole IP header is not unchanged: TTL and its checksum change, and fragmentation can change additional fields.
For ordinary forwarding, a router processes through the network layer. It does not deliver the transit message to a local UDP/TCP application.
Hosts implement all layers; routers need the lower three for forwarding. An ordinary layer-2 switch forwards within the LAN without replacing the frame’s source and destination MAC addresses. A frame can therefore reach its addressed next-hop interface through switches.

title: 9  Network stack
text:
4. IPv4 fragmentation

MTU and what is split
A link’s MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) limits the size of the network-layer PDU carried as link-layer payload. In these IPv4 problems:
\[
\boxed{\text{IP header}+\text{IP payload}\leq\text{MTU}}
\]
Ethernet headers and the FCS are outside this IP MTU.
If an IPv4 datagram is larger than the outgoing MTU, the sender or a router can fragment it, provided fragmentation is permitted.
Fragmentation splits the original IP payload, which includes any transport header. Every fragment receives its own IP header and is itself an IP datagram, carried in its own link-layer frame.
Reassembly occurs at the destination host’s IP layer, before delivery to UDP/TCP. Intermediate forwarding routers do not normally reassemble transit datagrams. If a fragment is missing, the complete original datagram cannot be delivered upward.


Header fields needed for calculations
Assume a 20-byte IPv4 header without options unless stated otherwise.
IPv4’s IHL measures the header length in 4-byte words:
\[
\text{IHL}=5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H=20\text{ bytes}.
\]







Field
Meaning for fragmentation




Total Length
This fragment’s IP header + its IP payload, in bytes


Identification / ID
16-bit value shared by all fragments of the original datagram


DF — Don’t Fragment
1: fragmentation forbidden; 0: permitted


MF — More Fragments
1: more original payload follows this fragment; 0: this is the final fragment


Fragment Offset
Where this fragment’s payload begins within the original IP payload, measured in 8-byte units


IHL / header length
Determines how much MTU space this fragment’s IP header occupies



The reserved flag is zero. An initially unfragmented datagram has offset 0 and MF = 0. When fragmenting it, all fragments keep its ID; DF must be 0.
ID is not globally unique by itself. Reassembly groups fragments using:
\[
\text{source IP, destination IP, protocol and ID}.
\]
Offsets place the payload bytes in their correct positions.
If DF = 1 and a forwarding router cannot fit the datagram onto the outgoing link, it drops it and normally reports ICMP “fragmentation needed” to the sender.


Why non-final payload lengths must be multiples of eight
Suppose the first fragment carries \(p_1\) bytes of original IP payload. The second begins at byte \(p_1\), so its offset field must contain:
\[
\mathrm{Offset}_2=\frac{p_1}{8}.
\]
This must be an integer. The same reasoning applies at every subsequent boundary. Therefore, every non-final fragment payload must be a multiple of eight bytes. The IPv4 specification explicitly defines the offset in these 8-byte units. rfc-editor.org
The final payload can have a different length: its starting position still lies on an 8-byte boundary, but no subsequent fragment needs to start after it.
The alignment rule concerns payload lengths, not Total Lengths including IP headers.


A reusable procedure
This procedure assumes an initially unfragmented datagram, constant header length \(H\), and maximal payloads for non-final fragments.
Let:

\(L\): original IP Total Length;
\(H\): IP header size;
\(M\): outgoing MTU;
\(D=L-H\): original IP payload size.

If application data size is given instead, first add the transport header to obtain \(D\), then add the IP header to obtain \(L\).
A stated “IP datagram length” includes its IP header, unless the question explicitly says payload.
Step 1 — Check necessity and permission.
If \(L\leq M\), fragmentation is unnecessary. If \(L>M\), check DF.
Step 2 — Calculate fragment payload capacity.
\[
\boxed{C=M-H}
\]
Step 3 — Round down for a non-final payload.
\[
\boxed{
F=8\left\lfloor\frac{M-H}{8}\right\rfloor
}
\]
Step 4 — Distribute the original payload.

While the remaining payload exceeds \(C\), emit a fragment with \(F\) payload bytes.
Once the remainder is at most \(C\), put all of it in the final fragment.
Count the resulting fragments.

The final fragment may carry up to \(C\), even if this is slightly larger than \(F\). Do not force its length to be a multiple of eight or mechanically calculate the count as \(\lceil D/F\rceil\).
Step 5 — Fill the fields.
If fragment \(i\) has payload length \(p_i\) and begins after \(b_i\) bytes of original payload:
\[
\mathrm{TotalLength}_i=H+p_i,
\]
\[
\mathrm{Offset}_i=\frac{b_i}{8},
\qquad
b_i=\sum_{j<i}p_j.
\]
Set MF = 1 except on the final fragment, where MF = 0. Keep the original ID for every fragment.
Step 6 — Check the result.

Payload lengths sum to \(D\).
Every Total Length is at most \(M\).
Non-final payloads are divisible by eight.
Offsets refer to original payload positions and count no IP headers.



Short worked example
An IPv4 datagram has Total Length 1700 bytes, ID = 91, DF = 0, and a 20-byte header. The outgoing MTU is 622 bytes.
\[
D=1700-20=1680,
\qquad
C=622-20=602,
\]
\[
F=8\lfloor602/8\rfloor=600.
\]
Send 600 bytes, then another 600. The remaining 480 fit into the final fragment.

\]
The first two fragments leave two bytes of MTU capacity unused because a 602-byte non-final payload would violate alignment.


Fragmentation versus transport segmentation







TCP segmentation
IPv4 fragmentation




Divides transport stream data into TCP segments
Divides one existing IP datagram’s payload


Each segment receives its own TCP header
Each fragment receives its own IP header

In today’s UDP examples, the UDP header is at the beginning of the original IP payload and appears only in the first fragment. Later fragments carry subsequent portions of that payload.
UDP receives the complete reassembled UDP datagram at the destination.

title: 9  Network stack
text:
5. Common exam traps

Putting headers in sender-processing order instead of their final frame order: the link header is outermost.
Treating IP payload as application data alone: it includes the transport header.
Addressing a remote data datagram to the gateway’s IP instead of the remote host’s IP.
Using the remote host’s MAC on the first LAN, or preserving MAC addresses through router hops.
Claiming the entire IP header remains unchanged: TTL and its checksum change.
Treating ports as PIDs, or assuming one TCP server port identifies one established connection.
Subtracting Ethernet overhead from the IP MTU, or forgetting to subtract the IP header.
Using \(M-H\) directly for non-final payloads without checking divisibility by eight.
Counting IP headers in offsets, or writing ordinary byte offsets into the Fragment Offset field.
Copying the UDP header into every fragment; treating MF = 0 as proof that reassembly is complete.

In this scenario, that gateway MAC happens to be the same MAC B observed as the incoming frame’s source—but it is used as the local next-hop address.



Exercise 2 — One server port, several TCP connections

2(a) — Connection identification
Using the order
\[

\text{destination IP},\text{destination port}),
\]
the connection identifiers are:

K1 versus K2: distinguished by the source IP address.
K1 versus K3: distinguished by the source port.



2(b) — Demultiplexing
The student’s claim is incorrect.
For an established TCP connection, the operating system uses the complete four-tuple, not the destination port alone. All three connections can therefore share server port 8080 while using distinct connection sockets.







Socket
Role

Established connection socket

Accepting a connection does not require assigning a different server port: the remote IP and port distinguish connections sharing the same local endpoint.


2(c) — Another transport protocol
The receiving stack processes the frame as follows:

Ethernet: the EtherType indicates IPv4, so the frame’s payload is passed to IPv4.
IPv4: destination IP 203.0.113.40 identifies S. Protocol = 17 selects UDP.
UDP: destination port 8080, together with the destination IP, selects the receiving UDP service/socket.

The datagram is not delivered to K1–K3. Those are TCP connections. TCP and UDP have separate port namespaces, so TCP port 8080 and UDP port 8080 can coexist.


2(d) — Port versus PID
No. Port 51000 is a transport-layer identifier; a PID identifies an operating-system process.
Their numbers are assigned independently. A process can use multiple sockets and ports, and its PID cannot generally be inferred from a packet’s port number.



Exercise 3 — Fragmenting one UDP datagram

3(a) — Original lengths
Application data:

\]
Adding the UDP header gives:
\[
\text{UDP datagram length}
=3995+8
=\boxed{4003\text{ bytes}}.
\]

\]

\[

3(b) — Fragment capacity
The MTU includes the IP header, so the maximum fragment payload capacity is:
\[

\]
A non-final payload must be divisible by eight:
\[

=8\cdot125
=\boxed{1000\text{ bytes}}.
\]
The capacities differ because 1003 is not divisible by eight.
A 1003-byte first payload would make the next fragment start at byte 1003, requiring offset \(1003/8=125.375\), which cannot be represented in the integer Fragment Offset field.
The final fragment can carry 1003 bytes, because no later fragment needs to start after it.

The final payload being larger than 1000 is intentional. Only non-final payloads require alignment.
A split into \(1000+1000+1000+1000+3\) would also satisfy IPv4 alignment, but would use an unnecessary fifth fragment and would not follow the exercise’s instruction to use the entire remainder once it fits.


3(d) — Header overhead
The sum of the fragments’ IP Total Lengths is:
\[
3\cdot1020+1023
=\boxed{4083\text{ bytes}}.
\]
Equivalently:
\[

+4\cdot20\text{ header bytes}
=4083.

=\boxed{60\text{ additional IP-header bytes}}.

\[

3(e) — Transport and reassembly
Fragments do not receive fresh UDP headers.
The original UDP header occupies bytes 0–7 of the original IP payload, so it appears only in fragment 1.
That fragment contains:

8 bytes of UDP header;
992 bytes of application data.

The remaining fragments contain subsequent application data. Each fragment receives its own IP header.
Reassembly takes place at the destination host’s IP layer. After successful reassembly, UDP receives the original 4003-byte UDP datagram:
\[
8\text{ header bytes}+3995\text{ application bytes}.
\]
UDP then delivers the 3995 application bytes to the receiving application.


3(f) — Two independent variants
3(f)(1) — The fragment with MF = 0 arrives first
The destination cannot yet deliver the complete message.
MF = 0 identifies the fragment containing the end of the original payload. It does not indicate that all preceding fragments have arrived.
Here, fragment 4 supplies bytes 3000–4002, but bytes 0–2999 are still missing. IP must wait for complete reassembly before delivering the UDP datagram upward.
3(f)(2) — The original datagram has DF = 1
The original IP datagram is 4023 bytes, exceeding the outgoing MTU of 1023 bytes.
Because DF = 1 prohibits fragmentation, R must drop the datagram and normally send an ICMP “fragmentation needed” error to the original sender.

title: 10  Subnetting, forwarding and routing algorithms
text:
1. IPv4 addresses, prefixes and masks
Allow approximately 60–90 minutes for the theory and worked examples, followed by 90–110 minutes for the three exercises. Solutions are omitted.
The connection throughout is:
Subnets define address ranges; prefixes describe those ranges in forwarding tables; routing computes paths; each path supplies a next hop; forwarding selects that next hop using the destination address.
An IPv4 address contains 32 bits, written as four 8-bit octets in dotted decimal.
In a.b.c.d/p:
The prefix length belongs to the network configuration: an address alone does not determine its subnet.
Increasing the prefix length fixes more bits, making the represented block smaller. When a parent /p is divided into equal /q subnets, the additional \(q-p\) prefix bits distinguish those subnets.
Historically, a Class-C network meant /24. For these calculations, use the explicitly given CIDR prefix.

title: 10  Subnetting, forwarding and routing algorithms
text:
the first \(p\) bits form the network/prefix part (Netzanteil, Netz-ID);
the remaining \(h=32-p\) bits form the host part (Hostanteil, Host-ID), identifying an interface within that subnet.





Construct a subnet mask from scratch
A subnet mask contains \(p\) leading ones followed by \(32-p\) zeros.
Its ones retain the network bits; its zeros remove the host bits when performing bitwise AND.

Write 255 for every complete group of eight prefix bits.
If \(r\) prefix bits remain in the next octet, write \(r\) leading ones there.
Fill all remaining bits with zeros.

For \(1\le r\le7\), the partial octet has decimal value:
\[
256-2^{8-r}.
\]










Prefix
Mask construction
Dotted-decimal mask
Host bits
Total addresses




/20
16 ones, then 11110000, then 8 zeros
255.255.240.0
12
4096


/24
24 ones, then 8 zeros
255.255.255.0
8
256


/27
24 ones, then 11100000
255.255.255.224
5
32



For the reverse conversion, count the leading ones, including the complete 255 octets.
For example:
\[
255.255.252.0
\]
contains \(8+8+6=22\) leading ones because:
252 = 11111100
Therefore, its prefix is /22.
A CIDR mask must contain contiguous leading ones. 255.255.250.0 is invalid because 250 = 11111010.


Total addresses versus usable host addresses
For a /p block:
\[
h=32-p,\qquad S=2^h\text{ total addresses}.
\]
For an ordinary IPv4 LAN in this unit, exclude:

the network address, whose host bits are all zero;
the broadcast address, whose host bits are all one.

Therefore:
\[
\text{usable interface addresses}=2^h-2.
\]
A router’s LAN interface also consumes one usable address. If a requirement counts only end devices, add the necessary router interfaces before sizing the subnet.
Follow the question’s convention. Sheet 10 A2 uses ordinary host counting; A3 explicitly permits all addresses.
For ordinary point-to-point links here, use /30: four total addresses and two usable addresses. A /31 can support a point-to-point link under a separate convention; do not silently switch conventions. A /32 represents one address, often used as a host route.
Thus, \(2^h-2\) is the ordinary LAN rule, not a universal rule for every prefix length.


Network address, host ID and represented range
For address \(A\) and mask \(M\):
\[
N=A\mathbin{\&}M,
\]
\[
H=A\mathbin{\&}(\text{32-bit complement of }M).
\]
Here:

\(N\) is the full network address;
\(H\) is the host part with all network bits cleared.

As integers:
\[
H=A-N.
\]
Once \(N\) and block size \(S\) are known:
\[
B=N+S-1,
\]
where \(B\) is the broadcast address for an ordinary subnet.
Its usable range is:
\[
N+1\quad\text{through}\quad B-1.
\]
Address arithmetic treats the address as one 32-bit integer, carrying between octets when necessary. For an aggregate prefix, \(B\) is simply its highest represented address: an aggregate need not describe one physical broadcast subnet.
Worked example: 192.0.2.149/27.
Only the last octet matters:
Address:  10010101   (149)
Mask:     11100000   (224)
AND:      10000000   (128)
Host:     00010101   (21)
The five host bits are 10101.
Therefore:



Quantity
Result




Network
192.0.2.128/27


Host ID
21


Broadcast
192.0.2.159


Usable range
192.0.2.129–192.0.2.158


Usable addresses
30





A faster block-boundary method
In the octet containing the prefix boundary, calculate:
\[
\Delta=256-\text{mask octet}.
\]
Then:
\[
\text{network octet}
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{\text{address octet}}{\Delta}
\right\rfloor\Delta.
\]
Earlier octets stay unchanged. Later network-address octets become zero; later broadcast-address octets become 255.
For 172.22.77.203/20:

mask: 255.255.240.0;
relevant octet: the third;
increment: \(256-240=16\);
77 belongs to the interval 64–79.

Therefore:
\[
\text{network}=172.22.64.0/20,
\]
\[
\text{broadcast}=172.22.79.255.
\]
Notice that the host part extends across two octets. Its numerical host ID cannot be determined from the last octet alone.


Are two addresses in the same subnet?
Under a specified mask \(M\), addresses \(A\) and \(C\) belong to the same subnet exactly when:
\[
(A\mathbin{\&}M)=(C\mathbin{\&}M).
\]
Compare their masked network addresses, not merely their first three decimal octets.

title: 10  Subnetting, forwarding and routing algorithms
section: 2. Subnet allocation: capacity, alignment and VLSM
text:
2. Subnet allocation: capacity, alignment and VLSM
VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking) allocates differently sized subnets within one parent block.
Each ordinary subnet receives a complete power-of-two block, including its network and broadcast addresses.

Reusable allocation procedure

Establish whether requirements mean total addresses or usable interface addresses, and whether gateways are included.
For \(H\) ordinary usable addresses, choose the smallest integer \(h\ge2\) satisfying:
\[
2^h-2\ge H.
\]
If all addresses are explicitly usable, use \(2^h\ge H\).
Calculate:
\[
p=32-h,\qquad S=2^h.
\]
Allocate larger blocks first, choosing free, correctly aligned starts.
Record each network, mask, complete range and usable range.
Check containment within the parent, non-overlap and capacity.

Count unused addresses using complete allocated block sizes, rather than requested host counts.


Why alignment matters
A network address must have all host bits zero.
Equivalently, its 32-bit integer value must be divisible by its block size.
A /26 contains 64 addresses. Within one /24, its possible last-octet starts are:
\[
0,\ 64,\ 128,\ 192.
\]
A proposed start .96/26 actually denotes the block beginning at .64; it does not create a /26 beginning at .96.
Short example. Within 192.0.2.0/24, two networks require 50 and 20 usable interface addresses.
Their minimum sizes are:
\[
64-2\ge50\quad\Rightarrow\quad /26,
\]
\[
32-2\ge20\quad\Rightarrow\quad /27.
\]
Allocate:

192.0.2.0/26;
192.0.2.64/27.

Both starts are aligned and the ranges do not overlap.
If the smaller subnet were allocated at .0/27 first, the /26 would need to start at .64, leaving a gap. Largest-first allocation makes packing simpler.
For equal-size subdivision:
\[
\text{number of `/q` subnets within `/p`}
=
2^{q-p}.
\]
No additional two subnets are subtracted under the conventions used here.


Sheet 10 A3’s special allocation notation
A3 also permits large prefix minus smaller prefix, with all addresses usable.
For example:
10.30.6.0/25 - 10.30.6.124/30
allocates .0–.123 to one address set and reserves .124–.127 separately.
The remainder contains:
\[
128-4=124\text{ addresses}.
\]
It is not itself one CIDR block. This is the exercise’s address-set notation rather than ordinary one-prefix LAN allocation.
A forwarding entry for the covering /25 still matches the reserved /30. If the smaller range needs another output, add a more-specific /30 entry.
Subtracting an allocated range does not change the bits matched by the original prefix.

title: 10  Subnetting, forwarding and routing algorithms
text:
3. Prefixes, aggregation and longest-prefix matching
A forwarding-table entry associates a destination address range with an outgoing interface and, for a remote destination, a neighboring next-hop router.
A destination \(A\) matches N/p if:
\[
A\mathbin{\&}M_p=N.
\]
Use a canonical network address \(N\), with zero host bits.

Convert an address range into one prefix
For an inclusive range \(L\) through \(U\):

Calculate \(S=U-L+1\).
Check that \(S\) is a power of two, say \(2^h\).
Check that \(L\) is aligned: its last \(h\) bits must be zero.
The exact prefix is then:
\[
L/(32-h).
\]

Alternatively, compare the endpoints’ binary forms. After their common leading bits:

the lower endpoint must contain only zeros;
the upper endpoint must contain only ones.

For example, 192.0.2.64–192.0.2.127 contains 64 addresses and starts at a multiple of 64.
Its last octets are:
64:   01000000
127:  01111111
They share two leading bits, giving \(24+2=26\) prefix bits:
192.0.2.64/26
An arbitrary interval may require several prefixes. The common leading bits of its endpoints can describe a larger containing block, rather than the exact interval.


Route aggregation
Two equal-size prefixes can merge into a prefix one bit shorter when they are the two aligned halves of that parent.
For example:
192.0.2.64/27
192.0.2.96/27
merge into:
192.0.2.64/26
Adjacency alone is insufficient: .32/27 and .64/27 are not the aligned halves of one /26.
For straightforward forwarding aggregation, the merged destinations must use the same next hop/output. More-specific exceptions can override an aggregate where explicitly required.


Longest-prefix matching
Among all matching entries, select the entry with the greatest prefix length.
Use this procedure:

Identify every prefix containing the destination.
Compare their prefix lengths.
Select the largest length and use its output/next hop.

A longer prefix fixes more destination bits, describing a smaller, more specific subset. This supports exceptions within broader routes.



Destination prefix
Output




0.0.0.0/0
WAN


10.8.0.0/16
A


10.8.12.0/24
B


10.8.12.128/25
C



Examples:

10.8.12.170 matches all four entries: /25 selects C.
10.8.12.20 matches the first three: /24 selects B.
10.8.13.20 matches /16 and /0: select A.

The /0 entry fixes no bits and matches every destination. It is the default route.
If nothing matches and there is no default, there is no forwarding route.
For a paper table scanned until the first match, sort entries by decreasing prefix length. The underlying rule remains longest-prefix matching, regardless of physical row order.
Adding a narrower exception does not shrink the broader prefix’s represented range. It changes which destinations actually select that broader entry.

title: 10  Subnetting, forwarding and routing algorithms
text:
4. Routing versus forwarding
Forwarding (Weiterleitung) is a router’s local per-packet action: inspect the destination, match a prefix and select an output.
Routing (Wegewahl) computes or learns the path information used to populate those entries.
For example, routing establishes that the cheapest path to the router serving 10.50.4.0/24 begins through neighbor \(a\). The source installs:
10.50.4.0/24 → next hop a
Forwarding subsequently matches packet destinations against that entry.







Distinction
Meaning




Mask/prefix calculation versus path calculation
Which addresses belong together versus which sequence of links reaches them


Destination prefix versus next hop
Ultimate destination range versus adjacent router receiving the packet next


Longest prefix versus shortest path
Most specific matching destination range versus lowest sum of link costs


Predecessor versus next hop
Last node before the destination versus first node after the source



Longest-prefix matching does not run Dijkstra for every packet.
Among entries for different matching prefixes, it chooses the most specific prefix even if a broader entry has a smaller route cost.
